books.section: Topic 7.6 World War I: Home Front
United States and World War I (1914-1921)
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

primary_sources: John E. Sheridan, "Food is Ammunition—Don't waste it" poster, 1917

stimulus.text: The poster shows a large basket of vegetables and fruit in the foreground. Behind it, the silhouettes of soldiers on horseback appear under an American flag. Large lettering reads: "Food is Ammunition — Don't waste it." Small print at the bottom reads: "UNITED STATES FOOD ADMINISTRATION." The poster was drawn by John E. Sheridan in 1917.
stimulus.source_note: Poster by John E. Sheridan, 1917, U.S. Food Administration, public domain.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, John E. Sheridan poster, 1917, public domain
stem: The Food Administration's approach in the poster is most similar to the approach of which other wartime agency?

options.text: the Supreme Court in Schenck v. United States
options.misconception: The Court decided a case and set a legal rule; it did not manage the wartime economy.

options.text: the Senate in its debate over the League of Nations
options.misconception: The Senate debated a treaty; it did not manage the wartime economy.

options.text: the American Federation of Labor in the 1919 steel strike
options.misconception: The steel strike came after the war and was a fight between workers and owners, not a government agency.

options.text: the War Industries Board in working with business to raise production

rationales.A: The Court decided a case and set a legal rule. It did not manage the wartime economy.
rationales.B: The Senate debated a treaty. It did not manage the wartime economy.
rationales.C: The steel strike came after the war and was a fight between workers and owners, not a government agency.
rationales.D: Both were new wartime agencies that steered the economy by working with farmers and business leaders instead of taking their property over.
rationales.general:
1. Name the Food Administration's approach: steer production and conservation by working with farmers and families.
2. Ask which other agency worked the same way. The War Industries Board worked with business to raise production.
3. Rule out the options that are not wartime economic agencies at all.
Remember: compare agencies by how they worked, not just by the war they served in.
